We need to make this happen ASAP! https://mobile.twitter.com/RaoulGMI/status/1364896784355627011 This message isn’t going to go away. Ethereum needs to have concrete dates to stop trashing the environment NOW or we are going to get eviscerated by the public conversation that is coming. This is URGENT folks. <@!438324482306998273> thanks for the call of action, but please don't use caps or go off-topic. We're well aware of the situation and actively building the replacement. eth2 call in 20 minutes we'll be discussion merge specs today and there are people working on the merge daily Livestream link? one mnute I wouldn't mind a link as well, assuming you have room for one more. https://youtu.be/yrDVhoTg5XU I've heard it mentioned a few times, can anyone point me to discussion on capping the # of validators? https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-specs/issues/2137 Call notes https://hackmd.io/@benjaminion/B1BZs7SMO ETH2 currently trails ETH1 right? That is, ETH2 is validating blocks from `n` minutes ago or something? If so, what is `n`? 2048 Eth1 blocks Hypothetically, what happens if there is a 2048 block ETH1 reorg? (I'm aware of how unlikely that is) Ethereum is dead if that can happen. The 2048 is not so much about fork resistance as allowing time for devs to fix any issues if something bad happens on Eth1 or to the deposit contract. In theory, if miners are angry *enough* about PoS cutting out their business they could (in theory) coordinate such an attack. It would not be profitable for them, more of a 🖕 on the way out the door. To answer your question - there is a separate voting process in Eth2 on Eth1 blocks. If clients disagree, because they are following different Eth1 chains, then no new validators can be onboarded. I wonder if, as an iterative step toward The Merge, we could introduce finality into ETH1 clients where they will refuse to reorg past ETH2 finality. This would require all ETH1 clients to connect to ETH2 clients, which would introduce the bi-directional communication we'll need for The Merge, and it would protect us from a particular class of miner attacks around The Merge and take some amount of power away from miners to disrupt the chain. You could probably use it to spin up some costless validators too (same as a double-spend). In particular I like the idea of getting the bi-directional connection up and running before it is on the hot path (The Merge). And this gives ETH1 clients *something* to use that connection for. This used to be in the plan. But iirc was dropped as it is a significant engineering project, and it was thought more expedient to put the resources into accelerating the Merge. My recollection on this is hazy, though. Hmm, is there extra engineering required for this plan? It feels like it just breaks up engineering work that already needs to be done? ETH1 needs to talk to ETH2 for The Merge, so that work has to be done either way and that feels like the bulk of the work here. Adding logic to the fork choice rule of ETH1 clients *feels* fairly simple, but maybe I'm missing something? > ETH1 needs to talk to ETH2 for The Merge, so that work has to be done either way and that feels like the bulk of the work here. Not really. The bridge would need at least BLS precompiles in Eth1 - an Eth2 light client - as well as fork choice changes. The beauty of the executable beacon chain is that it side-steps all that. Oh, The Merge doesn't require ETH1 clients to implement BLS precompiles? I had heard otherwise. Why is an ETH2 light client required? Is this information incorrect? https://discord.com/channels/595666850260713488/800773302213279784/807258676900790292 It would be required if shards shipped before the merge to allow eth1 apps e.g. rollups to use shards as the data layer > Why is an ETH2 light client required? This is how an Eth1 node learns about the state of Eth2, and can prove things about it. It needs to be able to verify BLS signatures to do so. Maybe not in the EVM, but certainly in the client. After the merge, they are tightly coupled, and no light client is needed on the Eth1 side. > Oh, The Merge doesn't require ETH1 clients to implement BLS precompiles? I had heard otherwise. No, the Merge itself does not. As per Mikhail, making shards visible in Eth1 does require Eth1 to know about BLS signatures. Perhaps I'm misunderstanding The Merge. I thought the plan was that as-of The Merge, everyone would need to run both an ETH1 client and an ETH2 client. Is this incorrect? > as-of The Merge, everyone would need to run both an ETH1 client and an ETH2 client. Is this incorrect? This is correct. As I said, at that point they are tightly coupled. Pre Merge, however, this is not the case. I'm arguing that we should try to break apart The Merge into more iterative steps. It feels like we could introduce the coupling in a limited capacity by having ETH1 get finality from ETH2 prior to the merge, and it wouldn't create *new work*. I would say that in a different way. After the merge there will be an upgraded ethereum client which is connected to both, the consensus (beacon chain) and application (mainnet) networks. Depending on the implementation it may be two pieces of software which were previously called eth2-client and eth1-engine or a single piece of software connected to both chains That aligns with my understanding. The key component here is that at the point of The Merge, ETH1 clients need to communicate with a PoS client in some way (whether that is internal due to having one baked in, or via network connection to a PoS validator). So between now and The Merge, ETH1 clients need to add that functionality. It isn't necessary to *wait* to add that functionality until The Merge itself, we could add that functionality before The Merge so it is done and tested in production when The Merge happens. At the point of merge the responsibility of keeping the head of the chain is moved to the consensus layer. I.e. beacon chain client will keep track of blocks and feed them to the application client. It does not imply bi-directional communication > it wouldn't create new work. But it would: (a) building an Eth2 light client into Eth1 clients, and (b) modifying Eth1's fork choice rule, with all the testing and governance around that. Neither of these are needed after the Merge. The fork choice rule changes I agree with. Can you help me better understand the need for an ETH2 light client that isn't necessary with The Merge? Right, and I think we can't rely on security assumptions of light clients here, it would rather require the full client run by miners You mean the light client on Eth1 chain or ETH2 light client in general? What you just described sounds bi-directional to me? The application client will receive blocks from the beacon chain (consensus => application) and the application will will tell the beacon about execution results (application => consensus). Whatever Benjaminion is talking about. 🙂 I must be missing some core component here because in my mental model of The Merge, everyone runs Geth/Nethermind/OpenEthereum/Besu + Teku/Lighthouse/Prysm/Nimbus client and they are connected and talk to each other. (assuming no new application layer or consensus layer clients are authored and no one authors a combined one by The Merge) Right, but the communication is initiate by the consensus layer because application payload becomes a part of beacon block. Application layer won't be able to initiate communication with the consensus one as it is not needed I'm also assuming (and maybe this is incorrect) that the connection between application layer and consensus layer clients will be trusted as-of The Merge, similar to how it is today where the consensus layer client "trusts" the data it gets from the JSON-RPC calls it makes to the application layer client. Hmm, so as of The Merge, the application layer client disconnects from the internet and just processes whatever the consensus layer client asks it to (and updates state accordingly)? Let's say for now that it will be disconnected from block gossip only. Not from the entire network stack. For instance, transaction pool remains unchanged, application state sync is the responsibility of the application client as well and probably (yet we don't know for sure) chain history as well. Consensus client will be responsible for pointing to the head of the chain and keeping application layer updated with it Consensus Client => Application Client: "Give me what you think should be the next block." Application Client => Consensus Client: "Done, here you go!" Consensus Client => Application Client: "This block is the new head, update your database accordingly." excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content:
Let's get back to it now. One of the proposals for the merge was two-step transition. After the first step block production is kept by miners while beacon chain validators secures the chain by mandating that valid chain includes the most recent finalized block; i.e. this is the stage when validators provide safety while miners provide liveness to the chain and get rewards for this job. 

The second step is switching block production to validators. The nice part of this plan is that during switching off the miners there will be no ability for them to attack the network. The downside is the requirement to run the beacon chain client for every participant in the network and increased timeline of the whole transition. And then the question, if the amount of work (research, engineering, community, etc) to deliver the first step is near the same to deliver the merge, shouldn't we rather go straight to the end goal?

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content:
Is this is what you have in mind? Or anything more granular?
1) Make the mainnet respect beacon chain finality; no gain for the mainnet (as distance is too high); requirements: run the full beacon node alongside ethereum mainnet node
2) Reduce follow distance to 16 and minimal finality distance to 32; mainnet is secured by the beacon chain; requirements: beacon chain changes (eth1 poll)
3) Merge

excerpts.author: sky.cactus

It's primary purpose would be to iterate on The Merge instead of doing it all in one big push.
It's secondary purpose would be to protect against a malicious miner attack that wrecks PoS before it launches.

excerpts.author: m.kalinin
excerpts.content: There are two parameter actually, `ETH1_FOLLOW_DISTANCE` and `EPOCHS_PER_ETH1_VOTING_PERIOD`. We would need to reduce both to reduce the delay between the production of the block and its finalised state. If we reduce `EPOCHS_PER_ETH1_VOTING_PERIOD` to something like `4` (`128` slots) with the current voting algorithm the whole voting mechanism starts to be pretty insecure under `2/3` honest majority assumption. Hence the change of the voting algorithm to reduce the distance even lower. This analysis is provided here with alternative voting algorithms https://ethresear.ch/t/on-the-way-to-eth1-finality/7041

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: My past experience tells me that a large monolithic change is more risky than a series of smaller changes that achieves the same end result.  Thus, in an effort to reduce risk for users I would *rather* take the iterative path over the all-at-once path.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: As an example of how this could go wrong, we have 4 ETH1 clients and 4 ETH2 clients.  Any one of them could have a bug in any individual piece of code.  If we release small chunks of that code at a time and start exercising them, a bug may pop up in one or two of the clients that would cause them to fall out of sync while everyone else remained in sync.  If we release a dozen changes at once, then we could see a different bug crop up in each of the clients causing everyone to fall out of sync from everyone else.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: We can of course do lots of things to mitigate this risk (like extensive testing), but by releasing the code in pieces we are more likely to hit the bugs one at a time instead of all at once.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Also, since humans are the ones implementing these features and we need consensus, it is a bit easier to achieve if we are able to all focus on one piece at a time rather than all clients implementing all the things at once.
